Out-earning or outnumbering: Two routes to cooperation in the fixed-role trust game on structured populations
abstract: Trust underlies cooperation, but sustaining it is individually costly and difficult under rational self-interest. In the trust game, a trustor invests part of an endowment and a trustee returns a share of the multiplied proceeds. Under fixed roles on a square lattice, agents play only with orthogonal neighbors of opposite-roles, but mimic diagonal neighbors of the same-role, decoupling interaction from imitation networks. Trust that collapses in well-mixed populations can instead co-evolve with trustworthiness on the lattice within a narrow range of the return parameter under strong selection. Comparing update rules uncovers two distinct routes to cooperation. First, pairwise imitation depends on reciprocators (that is, reciprocating trustees) outperforming betrayers through local assortment, forming clusters of trustworthy trustees around generous trustors. In contrast, a neighborhood rule allows the local majority of reciprocators convert an isolated betrayer regardless of the payoff, outnumbering betrayers rather than out-earning them. This collective-recruitment route sustains trust-reciprocate interactions over a wider range of the return parameter. The two routes differ, however, in what they require: pairwise spread needs only cross-role assortment and still produces cooperation on a geometry-free degree-regular network, whereas collective recruitment does not survive that change. Degree heterogeneity adds no route of its own, and whether it leaves cooperation standing depends on which role carries it and on how payoffs are aggregated. Of the structures examined here, only the lattice supports both routes.

Mamba-MVQ: Aligning mixed-precision quantization with Mamba for efficient multimodal reasoning
abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have delivered remarkable gains in multimodal understanding and reasoning, yet their prohibitive computational and memory costs remain a major barrier to real-world deployment. We present Mamba-based Multimodal Vision-Language Quantization (Mamba-MVQ), a compact and efficient multimodal inference framework that unifies the linear-complexity Mamba architecture with alignment-aware mixed-precision quantization. The proposed method assigns higher precision to semantically critical cross-modal modules, such as visual projection layers, while aggressively quantizing less sensitive components, including the linear layers in Mamba blocks, to maximize compression without severely compromising performance. To mitigate cross-modal semantic degradation introduced by quantization, we further introduce an alignment-preserving calibration objective based on vision-language contrastive learning. Combined with dynamic token merging, Mamba-MVQ reduces inference cost from both architectural and token-level perspectives. Extensive experiments on OpenCompass and MMBench show that Mamba-MVQ reduces model memory to 23.8% of the full-precision baseline with only a 1.7% average accuracy drop, demonstrating an effective trade-off between efficiency and multimodal capability.

PREF-XAI: Preference-based personalized rule explanations of black-box machine learning models
abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has predominantly focused on generating model-centric explanations that approximate the behavior of black-box models. However, such explanations often overlook a fundamental aspect of interpretability: different users require different explanations depending on their goals, preferences, and cognitive constraints. Although recent work has explored user-centric and personalized explanations, most existing approaches rely on heuristic adaptations or implicit user modeling, lacking a principled framework for representing and learning individual preferences. In this paper, we consider Preference-Based Explainable Artificial Intelligence (PREF-XAI), a novel perspective that reframes explanation as a preferencedriven decision problem. Within PREF-XAI, explanations are not treated as fixed outputs, but as alternatives to be evaluated and selected according to user-specific criteria. In the PREF-XAI perspective, here we propose a methodology that combines rule-based explanations with formal preference learning. User preferences are elicited through a ranking of a small set of candidate explanations and modeled via an additive utility function inferred using robust ordinal regression. Experimental results on real-world datasets show that PREF-XAI can accurately reconstruct user preferences from limited feedback, identify highly relevant explanations, and discover novel explanatory rules not initially considered by the user. Beyond the proposed methodology, this work establishes a connection between XAI and preference learning, opening new directions for interactive and adaptive explanation systems.
